title: Composition and delegation

sources.locator: C++ Core Guidelines; living guidelines accessed 2026-07; provisions applicable to Composition and delegation
sources.claim: Composition builds behavior from owned or referenced components and is preferred when the relationship is has-a or implemented-in-terms-of rather than substitutable is-a.

canonicalExplanation.summary: There are two ways to reuse a class. **Inheritance** says "B **is a** kind of A" and can be used wherever an A is expected. **Composition** says "B **has an** A" (or is "implemented using" one): B holds an A as a member and **delegates** to it. Prefer composition whenever you don't need substitution. It exposes **only** what you choose (not every public method of A), keeps A replaceable, and avoids odd claims like "a Report is a Formatter". The cost is a few short **forwarding** functions, which is usually a feature: they document exactly what B offers.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner writes `class Report : public Formatter` to reuse its format() code. Soon every Formatter method (set_locale, reset_buffer...) is callable on Report objects, and a function taking `Formatter&` accepts Reports, which makes no sense. A Report owns a Formatter component and delegates formatting without claiming that a Report is a kind of Formatter. In this lesson you'll refactor an inheritance-shaped design into composition when substitution is not needed.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Class interface and invariants** (public operations protect state) and **unique_ptr, shared_ptr and non-owning access** (owning members).

sections.heading: The distinction: has-a with delegation vs is-a
Leaky interfaces

includes: Refactor inheritance used only for reuse into owned components with delegation.

outcomes: Refactor an inheritance-shaped design into composition when substitution is not needed.

examples.title: A Report that has a Formatter
examples.situation: A Report owns a Formatter component and delegates formatting without claiming that a Report is a kind of Formatter.
walkthrough: **A Report owns a Formatter component:** fmt_ is a private member.
**Delegates formatting:** render() calls fmt_.format(v) for each value.
**Without claiming that a Report is a kind of Formatter:** functions taking Formatter& will no longer accept Reports, and set_locale isn't exposed.
examples.result: Report's interface is exactly add and render, and the design says what it means.

examples.title: The Stack that was a vector
examples.situation: `class Stack : public std::vector<int>` lets callers insert into the middle, breaking stack order.
walkthrough: A stack isn't substitutable for a vector: it has fewer, stricter operations.
Hold a std::vector<int> member and offer push, pop and top only.
Each method delegates in one line.
examples.result: The stack's invariant (last in, first out) can't be broken.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Inheritance is always the best reuse mechanism because composition requires writing forwarding methods.
misconceptions.correction: Inheritance claims substitutability and exposes the whole base interface. Composition reuses behaviour while exposing only chosen operations; short forwarding methods are a small, explicit cost.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The Stack that was a vector", which invariant did inheritance break?

analogy.example: Composition is like **a restaurant that has a dishwasher**. The restaurant uses it (delegates) but customers don't press the dishwasher's buttons. Inheritance would be declaring **"this restaurant is a dishwasher"**: now every dishwasher button is on the menu.
usefulFor: only chosen buttons on the menu
limitations: Restaurants can replace dishwashers; composed components are swappable too.
Some things really are a kind of another: that's when inheritance fits.

steps.explanation: The Report owns a Formatter component and its own data.
It delegates formatting to the component for each value.
A Report is not claimed to be a kind of Formatter.

nearTransfer.prompt: Classify each as is-a or has-a and justify: Car/Engine, Circle/Shape, Logger/File, Manager/Employee (in a payroll system), Playlist/std::vector.
scaffold: Can one be used everywhere the other is?

farTransfer.prompt: Refactor `class Stack : public std::vector<int>` into composition, write tests proving the stack only allows push, pop, top, size and empty, and then change the internal container to std::deque without changing any test.
scaffold: Tests use the public API only.

remediation.explanation: Before inheriting ask: **could every function that takes the base safely receive this class?** If not, or if you only want its code, **hold it as a member and delegate**.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The Stack that was a vector".

recap.summary: To refactor inheritance used only for reuse, check whether the relationship is has-a rather than substitutable is-a, hold the component as a private member, delegate to it through a small chosen interface, and keep public inheritance for types that truly substitute for their base.
